overview.intro:
Chapter 19 covers food made from cereals, flour, starch or milk: **infant formula** and other preparations of heading 1901, cake mixes and doughs, **pasta and noodles**, tapioca, **breakfast cereals**, and **bread, biscuits, cakes and pastry**. Its **111 tariff lines** run from Free on dry pasta, bread and sweet biscuits to $1.035/kg + 14.9% on over-quota infant formula and $1.128/kg on over-quota margarine cheese.

The U.S. imported **$16.12B** of these goods in 2025, and 71% of it was bakers' wares (heading 1905). **Canada** ($6.64B) and **Mexico** ($2.84B) supplied 59%, then **Italy** ($1.44B, mostly pasta) and **South Korea** ($684M, mostly noodles). On top of the base rate comes an **extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies — 10% in total for EU goods, 12.5% in total for South Korea, +10% for the UK and India, +12.5% for Türkiye and Thailand, +20% for China (+37.5% on dry pasta, noodles and bread under List 3) and +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt — except four Canadian sugar mix and dough lines (1901.20.25, .35, .60, .70) that pay a 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA. Tapioca is exempt for everyone.

Dairy- and sugar-containing preparations of heading 1901 are under **tariff-rate quotas**: a low rate inside the quota and a high per-kilogram rate above it, with separate FTA quotas for Canada, Australia, Colombia and others. Dry pasta from Italy and Türkiye also carries **antidumping and countervailing duties** set by producer, which are collected on top and are not in the rate grid.

productGroups.label: Malt extract; infant formula, mixes & doughs, dairy and cereal food preparations
productGroups.blurb: Infant formula (1901.10), cake and bread mixes and doughs (1901.20), malt extract, puddings and dairy or cereal food preparations (1901.90). Most lines with over 10% milk solids or over 10% cane or beet sugar are quota lines: 10%–17.5% inside the quota, up to $1.035/kg + 14.9% above it. Plain mixes are 8.5%, other food preparations 6.4%, ready-to-eat puddings Free.

productGroups.label: Pasta, noodles & couscous
productGroups.blurb: Dry pasta and noodles made only of pasta (1902.11.20, 1902.19.20) are Free; pasta with sauce, stuffed pasta (ravioli, dumplings), cooked and instant noodles (1902.30) and couscous pay 6.4%. Non-egg dry pasta from Italy and Türkiye also owes antidumping and countervailing duties.

productGroups.label: Tapioca and tapioca substitutes
productGroups.blurb: Tapioca and pearls from arrowroot, cassava or sago are Free; other starch substitutes pay 0.8¢/kg. Both are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties.

productGroups.label: Breakfast cereals, muesli, bulgur & prepared grains
productGroups.blurb: Corn flakes and puffed or roasted cereals (1904.10) pay 1.1%; muesli-type mixes of unroasted flakes 5.6% (airtight containers) or 14.9%; bulgur 14%; pre-cooked and other prepared grains (1904.90) 14%.

productGroups.label: Bread, pastry, cakes, biscuits & other bakers' wares
productGroups.blurb: Bread, pastry, cakes, sweet biscuits, cookies, crackers, waffles, wafers, gingerbread, rusks and crispbread are all Free. Only 1905.90.90 pays 4.5%: corn chips and similar savory snacks, pizza and quiche, communion wafers and rice paper.

workedExamples.title: Dry pasta from Italy
workedExamples.body: Non-egg dry pasta is Free under the general rate. For EU goods with a base rate under 10%, the 2026 Section 301 action charges 10% in total (9903.05.39), so a $100,000 container pays **$10,000**. Retail-size packs (up to 5 lb 4 oz) are also under the 1996 antidumping and countervailing duty orders, which CBP collects as cash deposits by producer: for example 2.65% (La Molisana) or 7.00% (Garofalo) antidumping from March 16, 2026, 5.21% for the other reviewed firms and 15.45% for firms never reviewed, plus a countervailing deposit such as 3.32% for De Matteis. Certified organic and gluten-free pasta are outside the orders.

workedExamples.title: Cookies from Canada
workedExamples.body: Sweet biscuits are Free. Cookies that meet the USMCA rule (a change from any other chapter, so flour and sugar may be imported) and are entered under USMCA pay **nothing** (9903.05.93). A non-qualifying shipment pays the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada (9903.05.29): $5,000 on $50,000. No Chapter 19 bakers' ware is on a Canada Section 338 list or the September 29, 2026 import bans.

workedExamples.title: Infant formula from Germany
workedExamples.body: Retail infant formula with over 10% milk solids that contains oligosaccharides has a 100-tonne yearly quota (Chapter 19 note 2): 17.5% inside it (1901.10.11), **$1.035/kg + 14.9%** above it. The quota is small, so most commercial shipments pay the over-quota rate. Because that rate already works out above 10%, the EU Section 301 rate adds nothing. A 1,000 kg, $20,000 shipment pays $1,035 + $2,980 = **$4,015**. FDA rules (21 CFR parts 106 and 107, and a new infant formula notification) apply before it can be sold.

workedExamples.title: Instant noodles from South Korea
workedExamples.body: Instant and other prepared noodles are 6.4%, Free under the U.S.–Korea FTA (KR). South Korea's Section 301 rate is 12.5% in total when the rate is lower (9903.05.71), so KORUS noodles pay **12.5%** — $6,250 on $50,000. From China the same noodles pay 6.4% + 12.5% + 25% (List 3) = 43.9%.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 19 base rate changed: 101 of the 111 lines are the same, and the other 10 are new statistical splits for certified organic products (dry pasta, cereals, sweet biscuits and bread) that carry their parent line's rate.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**; only tapioca (1903) is on its general exemption list. China pays more because older Section 301 duties stack on top (25% on dry pasta, noodles, bread and 1901.90.91 under List 3; 7.5% on the rest), and Brazil adds a separate 25%. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are still exempt**, but four Canadian sugar mix and dough lines pay the 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026 whether or not they qualify.

Separately, Commerce cut the antidumping deposit rates on **Italian pasta** in its final 2023–2024 review (March 16, 2026: 2.65%–7.00%, after a preliminary 91.74%) and set new countervailing rates on July 24, 2026.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 19 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 lists, the Canada Section 338 duties on four 1901.20 lines, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, the scheduled Nicaragua tariff, and the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on pasta from Italy and Türkiye. Infant formula policy (FDA) and quota rules are on Duty-saving rules. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 19 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 111 Chapter 19 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. Ten statistical lines are new — certified organic and other splits of 1902.19.20 (dry pasta, EU and non-EU), 1904.10.00 (prepared cereals), 1905.31.00 (sweet biscuits) and 1905.90.10 (bread and pastry) — and take their 8-digit parent's rate (Free or 1.1%).

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. CAFTA-DR originating goods are not covered (U.S. note 29). Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: Canada dairy import ban does not reach Chapter 19
changes.detail: From September 29, 2026 certain Canadian dairy products moved from the 50% Section 338 duty to an import ban (Proclamation 11062). The Annex names products in Chapters 4, 17 and 22 only; 1901.20.35, the one Chapter 19 line on the dairy duty list, still pays the 50% duty and is not banned.

changes.title: New reviews of the Italian pasta orders
changes.detail: Commerce initiated administrative reviews of the antidumping order on pasta from Italy for July 2025–June 2026 (A-475-818) and of the countervailing duty order for calendar 2025 (C-475-819). Current deposit rates stay in place until those reviews are final.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties take effect on four mix and dough lines
changes.detail: 50% on Canadian goods on three lists (9903.03.12–9903.03.14) took effect after a 3-day suspension lapsed. Four Chapter 19 lines are listed: 1901.20.35 on the dairy list (note 51(b)(2), 9903.03.13) and 1901.20.25, 1901.20.60 and 1901.20.70 on the list named for motor vehicles (note 51(b)(3), 9903.03.14). The duty applies even to goods entered under USMCA or Canada's USMCA quotas (U.S. note 51(a)).

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover Chapter 19
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). Only tapioca (1903.00.20, 1903.00.40) is on the general exemption list in U.S. note 52(b); religious-purpose bakers' wares are exempt by description (note 52(c)). EU goods pay 10% in total; Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5% in total. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Italian pasta: final countervailing duty rates for 2023
changes.detail: Commerce's final results of the 2023 review set countervailable subsidy rates of 3.32% for De Matteis and 3.21% for Granoro (Pastificio Attilio Mastromauro), and 3.32% for the two non-examined firms (Antiche Tradizioni di Gragnano, Pastificio Sgambaro). Cash deposits at these rates apply to entries from July 24, 2026; other firms keep their last rate.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). The exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)) covers tapioca (1903.00.20, 1903.00.40), and religious-purpose bakers' wares are exempt by description (note 50(a)(iii)). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S, S+) and the Canada and Mexico quota provisions in Chapter 98 subchapter XXIII still apply.

changes.title: Italian pasta: final antidumping rates far below the preliminary 91.74%
changes.detail: In the final results of the July 2023–June 2024 review, Commerce set dumping margins of 2.65% for La Molisana, 7.00% for Pastificio Lucio Garofalo and 5.21% for the 11 non-selected companies, replacing the preliminary 91.74%. These are the cash deposit rates from March 16, 2026; firms never individually reviewed keep the 15.45% all-others rate. Gluten-free and EU-certified organic pasta are outside the order.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Tapioca (1903.00.20, 1903.00.40) was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03), and religious-purpose bakers' wares were exempt by description (9903.03.04). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75) renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) makes most dutiable Chapter 19 lines Free for listed sub-Saharan countries; the over-quota dairy and sugar lines do not list D. GSP (SPI A, A*, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: FDA's infant formula transition plan guidance ran to October 18, 2025
changes.detail: The 2022 guidance let infant formula made abroad stay on the U.S. market under FDA enforcement discretion while makers worked toward full compliance; it was in effect until October 18, 2025. FDA's page lists six manufacturers (Bubs Australia, Danone, Kendal Nutricare, The a2 Milk Company, Reckitt/Mead Johnson and Vitaflo) whose products stayed in the plan and that filed new infant formula submissions by the July 15, 2025 deadline. This is an FDA marketing rule; it never changed the tariff.

changes.title: Italian pasta: preliminary antidumping rate of 91.74%
changes.detail: Commerce preliminarily found that the two examined Italian producers, La Molisana and Garofalo, had not cooperated and assigned 91.74% to them and to 11 other producers for July 2023–June 2024. It was a preliminary rate and was never collected as a deposit; the final results on March 16, 2026 replaced it with 2.65%–7.00%.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Tapioca was on the exemption list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Operation Stork Speed (FDA infant formula review)
changes.detail: HHS and FDA announced a review of infant formula nutrient requirements, more contaminant testing and steps to encourage new manufacturers, and kept the personal-importation policy for infant formula begun in 2022. No tariff change.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 19 goods were **$16.12B in 2025**, 1.6% less than the $16.38B of 2024 and up from $9.54B in 2020. Bakers' wares dominate: heading 1905 was $11.41B (71%), led by bread, pastry, cakes and snacks (1905.90, $7.64B) and sweet biscuits (1905.31, $2.48B). Pasta and noodles (heading 1902) were $1.93B, the preparations of heading 1901 $1.71B and breakfast cereals (1904) $1.02B.

**Canada** is by far the largest supplier ($6.64B, 41%), $5.24B of it bakers' wares; **Mexico** ($2.84B) is second, also mostly bakery ($2.48B). Both pay no extra duty on USMCA-qualifying goods. **Italy** ($1.44B) ships mostly pasta ($801M), which pays 10% under the 2026 Section 301 action plus producer-specific antidumping and countervailing deposits. **South Korea** ($684M) is mostly noodles ($348M). Infant formula and other retail preparations for infants and young children (1901.10) were $362M, down from $404M.

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24 and the Canada Section 338 duties from August 22, 2026); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on Chapter 19 goods depends as much on **where they come from** as on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico pay no extra duty** (except Canada's four Section 338 mix and dough lines, 50%), **EU goods pay 10%** in place of a lower base rate, **South Korea 12.5%** in total, most other large suppliers add 10% or 12.5%, **China adds 20% — 37.5% on dry pasta, noodles, dumplings and bread** — and Brazil adds 37.5%. Tapioca is exempt for everyone. On the dairy and sugar quota lines the cell shows the over-quota rate, except where an FTA sets its own quota: there it shows both tiers — for example Free within Canada's USMCA quotas and the over-quota rate plus 10% above them. Antidumping and countervailing duties on pasta from Italy and Türkiye are producer-specific and are not in the cells.

Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

Quota lines: where a product has an in-quota and an over-quota line, both are in the group; the over-quota rates (for example $1.035/kg + 14.9% on infant formula or 42.3¢/kg + 8.5% on sugar mixes) apply once the quota is filled, and the quota for articles over 65% sugar is set at none (Chapter 17 additional U.S. note 7).

FTA quota lines are priced per tier, the way the calculator asks. Australia: Free within its FTA dairy quota (9822.04.25), plus 12.5%. Colombia: Free within its sugar quota (9822.08.01), plus 12.5%.

Canada Section 338: the 50% on 1901.20.25, 1901.20.35, 1901.20.60 and 1901.20.70 is applied on both sides of the USMCA toggle, inside and above the quota, because U.S. note 51(a) applies it even when a special rate is claimed.

EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland: the 10% or 12.5% total applies when the base rate, or its ad valorem equivalent, is lower. Per-kilogram base rates are compared at the $10,000 / 1,000 kg test shipment ($10 per kg), so a cheaper product can end up paying only its per-kilogram rate.
Antidumping and countervailing duties (pasta from Italy and Türkiye) depend on the producer and are not in the cells.

Price-based special safeguard duties (Chapter 99 subchapter IV, 9904.04.50–9904.19.19) can add a per-kilogram charge to low-priced over-quota dairy and sugar goods; they do not apply to Canada, Mexico, Australia, South Korea, Colombia and the other FTA partners listed in subchapter IV note 1, and are not applied in the matrix.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 20, 29, 50, 51 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 21. The Section 301 general exemption list (note 52(b), 9903.05.86) has two Chapter 19 subheadings, 1903.00.20 and 1903.00.40 (tapioca); note 52(c) adds religious-purpose bakers' wares of 1905.90.10 and 1905.90.90 by description. The Brazil list (note 50(a)(ii)) has the same two tapioca lines, and note 50(a)(iii) the same religious-purpose goods. No Chapter 19 line is on a country exception list in note 52(j). Canada Section 338 (note 51(b)): 1901.20.35 is on the dairy list (b)(2) and 1901.20.25, 1901.20.60 and 1901.20.70 on list (b)(3); none is in the Proclamation 11062 import-ban Annex. China: List 3 (note 20(f)) covers 1901.90.91, 1902.19.20, 1902.19.40, 1902.20.00, 1902.30.00 and 1905.90.10, List 4A (note 20(s)(i)) the other Chapter 19 subheadings, and no China product exclusion still in force (note 20(vvv)–(www)) names a Chapter 19 product. Sweet biscuits (1905.31.00) and waffles and wafers (1905.32.00) appear only on the large-civil-aircraft lists (note 21(l), (n), 9903.89.37, 9903.89.43), which have not applied since 2021 (note 21(w)–(x)).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 19: Preparations of Cereals, Flour, Starch or Milk; Bakers' Wares — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Pasta, Bakery, Cereal & Infant Formula: FDA Rules, Quotas & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 19) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The FDA, USDA and CBP rules for each HTS Chapter 19 line — infant formula (21 CFR 106/107), FSVP, prior notice, labeling, dairy quota licenses, AD/CVD on pasta — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, other FTAs, quota entries, General Note 15, drawback and binding rulings.
keywords: usmca origin validation for baked goods
dairy tariff-rate quota mixes and doughs

tariffEngineering.intro:
Chapter 19 goods are food, so **FDA decides whether a shipment can be sold**: the foreign plant must be registered, prior notice must be filed before arrival, and the U.S. importer needs a foreign supplier verification program. **Infant formula** has its own regime — nutrient, quality control and labeling rules (21 CFR parts 106 and 107) and a new infant formula notification before marketing. Products with meat, such as some stuffed pasta and dumplings, can fall under USDA FSIS; in-quota margarine cheese needs a USDA dairy import license.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** or another **FTA**, enter dairy and sugar goods **inside a quota** (or under a **General Note 15** exclusion), and recover duty through **drawback** when the goods are exported. For Italian and Turkish dry pasta, the producer's antidumping and countervailing rate matters as much as the tariff. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty — 10% of value — plus the base rate; on the dairy and sugar quota lines, Free for Mexico at any quantity and Free inside Canada's USMCA quotas
levers.appliesTo: All 111 lines, for goods that meet the Chapter 19 rules of origin in General Note 11
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: The rules are generous for bakery and pasta — headings 1902–1905 need only a change from any other chapter, so imported flour, semolina and sugar are allowed — but dairy-based preparations of 1901.10, 1901.20 and 1901.90 may not use non-originating Chapter 4 dairy. Canada's quotas in 2026: 1,919 t of other dairy products (9823.08.02) and 9,600 t of sugar-containing products (9823.10.02, with a Canadian export certificate when USTR requires one); above them Canada pays the over-quota rate plus 10%. USMCA does not lift the 50% Section 338 duty on 1901.20.25, .35, .60 and .70 (U.S. note 51(a)). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin, Chapter 19)
USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim another free trade agreement
levers.saves: The base rate — for example 6.4% on noodles and stuffed pasta, 14% on bulgur, 14.9% on infant formula outside the quota system — on goods from Australia, Bahrain, Chile, Colombia, Israel, Jordan, South Korea, Morocco, Oman, Panama, Peru, Singapore and the CAFTA-DR countries
levers.appliesTo: Most dutiable lines; on the over-quota dairy and sugar lines only some partners are Free, others have their own quotas in Chapter 98 subchapter XXII (9822) or Chapter 99 — Australia's dairy quota 9822.04.25, Colombia's sugar quota 9822.08.01
levers.document: The origin proof each agreement requires (a certification or declaration of origin) and records to back it up.
levers.caveat: An FTA removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty for the 60 economies, which applies even when a special rate is claimed (U.S. note 52(a)); most of these partners are in the 60. For dairy preparations the FTA rules usually forbid non-originating Chapter 4 dairy. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020; AGOA (D) runs to December 31, 2026.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Enter dairy and sugar preparations inside the tariff-rate quota
levers.saves: The gap between the in-quota and over-quota rate: infant formula 17.5% instead of $1.035/kg + 14.9%; dairy preparations 16% instead of $1.035/kg + 13.6%; sugar mixes and doughs 10% instead of 42.3¢/kg + 8.5%; margarine cheese 10% instead of $1.128/kg
levers.appliesTo: The paired in-quota and over-quota lines in 1901.10, 1901.20 and 1901.90
levers.document: In-quota margarine cheese (1901.90.34) needs a USDA dairy import license (Chapter 4 additional U.S. note 23; 7 CFR part 6). The other quotas are filled at CBP in order of entry; check the quota status before shipping.
levers.caveat: The quotas are small: infant formula with oligosaccharides 100 t a year (Chapter 19 note 2); mixes and doughs 5,398 t from October 1 (note 3); "dairy products described in additional U.S. note 1 to chapter 4" 4,105,000 kg a year, shared with many other dairy goods (Chapter 4 note 10); articles over 10% sugar 64,709 t from October 1 (Chapter 17 note 8); articles over 65% sugar none (note 7). Mexico is outside these quotas because its goods are Free under USMCA. Low-priced over-quota goods can also owe a special safeguard duty (Chapter 99 subchapter IV) unless they come from an exempt FTA partner.

levers.title: Use a General Note 15 entry for samples, government or personal-use goods
levers.saves: The over-quota rate: these entries use the "described in general note 15" lines at the in-quota rate and are not counted against the quota
levers.document: Proof of the qualifying purpose: goods for a U.S. government agency; personal-use shipments of 5 kg or less; or samples, trade-fair, research or embassy goods that will not enter U.S. commerce, with written USDA approval presented at entry.
levers.caveat: Commercial goods do not qualify. Ask USDA for approval (identifying the product, quantity and use) before the goods ship.

levers.title: Check the producer's antidumping and countervailing rate before buying Italian or Turkish pasta
levers.saves: The difference between producer rates: Italian non-egg dry pasta pays antidumping deposits from 2.65% (La Molisana) to 15.45% (firms never reviewed), plus a countervailing deposit (for example 3.21%–3.32% for the firms reviewed for 2023); gluten-free and EU-certified organic pasta are outside the order
levers.appliesTo: Non-egg dry pasta in retail packs of 5 lb 4 oz or less (1902.19.20; 1901.90.91 for Italy) from Italy or Türkiye
levers.document: The producer and exporter names on the entry, and for organic pasta from Italy the EU organic certificate (USDA National Organic Program equivalence), kept and shown to CBP on request.
levers.caveat: Deposits are estimates; the final duty is set in later reviews (reviews of July 2025–June 2026 and of 2025 began September 4, 2026). Commerce's written scope, not the HTS number, decides what is covered.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported goods (or goods made from them) are exported or destroyed
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; antidumping and countervailing duties cannot be recovered by drawback, and CBP decides whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification — sweet biscuit (1905.31, Free) versus snack (1905.90.90, 4.5%), dry pasta (Free) versus pasta with sauce (6.4%), infant formula on a quota line versus 1901.10.29 — before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the recipe, milk-solids or sugar content, or packaging decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its ingredients (with percentages) and packaging.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a reformulated product may need a new one.

rules.title: Food facility registration for the foreign plant that makes, packs or holds the food
Prior notice of imported food, filed before the shipment arrives
Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP) kept by the U.S. importer
Food labeling: English label, ingredient list, Nutrition Facts, major allergens (wheat, milk, egg, soy, sesame)
Current good manufacturing practice and preventive controls at the foreign food plant
Food and color additives must be approved for the use (or GRAS); colors from the listed color additives
Standards of identity: products sold as "macaroni", "spaghetti", "noodles" or "enriched bread" must meet the federal standard
Canned pasta and other shelf-stable low-acid or acidified foods: plant registration and process filing

Infant formula: cGMP, quality control and records (21 CFR 106), nutrient, labeling and exempt-formula rules (21 CFR 107), and a new infant formula notification at least 90 days before marketing (FD&C Act sec. 412). The 2022 enforcement-discretion transition plan for formula made abroad ran to October 18, 2025

In-quota margarine cheese (1901.90.34) needs a dairy import license

groups.label: Malt extract; infant formula, mixes & doughs, dairy and cereal food preparations
groups.note: Infant formula (1901.10) follows 21 CFR parts 106 and 107 and needs an FDA new infant formula notification. Lines with over 10% milk solids or over 10% cane or beet sugar are quota lines (Chapter 4 note 10, Chapter 17 notes 7–8, Chapter 19 notes 2–3); in-quota margarine cheese needs a USDA license. 1901.20.25, .35, .60 and .70 from Canada pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Pasta, noodles & couscous
groups.note: Non-egg dry pasta from Italy and Türkiye is under antidumping and countervailing duty orders. Products labeled macaroni, spaghetti or noodles must meet 21 CFR part 139; canned pasta is a low-acid food; ravioli or dumplings with meat can be FSIS products.

groups.label: Tapioca and tapioca substitutes
groups.note: Tapioca is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties (only China's 7.5% List 4A applies).

groups.label: Breakfast cereals, muesli, bulgur & prepared grains
groups.note: Products with over 6% cocoa (defatted basis) or fully coated with chocolate are heading 1806, not 1904 (Chapter 19 note 3).

groups.label: Bread, pastry, cakes, biscuits & other bakers' wares
groups.note: Breads labeled "enriched" must meet the standard in 21 CFR part 136. Pizza, quiche and other bakers' wares with meat can be FSIS products. Religious-purpose communion wafers are exempt from the Section 301 duties by description.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. FDA and USDA requirements depend on the product's ingredients and form; check the agency before each new product, CBP for quota status before each quota-sensitive shipment, and Commerce's current deposit rate before each pasta purchase from Italy or Türkiye.

seo.title: Chapter 19 Tariff FAQ: HS Codes & U.S. Tariffs for Biscuits, Pasta, Noodles, Bread, Cereal & Infant Formula | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about HTS Chapter 19: the HS code for biscuits, cookies, pasta, instant noodles, bread, cake, breakfast cereal and infant formula — and the U.S. tariff on each by country in 2026, including the Italian pasta duties.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing Chapter 19 goods into the U.S. — HS codes, tariffs by country, quota rules and the pasta antidumping duties. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Bakers' wares are 71% of Chapter 19 imports, and almost all of them — bread, cookies, cakes, pastry, crackers, wafers — have a Free base rate; only snack chips, pizza and quiche (1905.90.90) pay 4.5%.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: 10% in total for the EU, 12.5% in total for South Korea, +10% or +12.5% for most other large suppliers, +20% for China (+37.5% on pasta, noodles and bread) and +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying goods pay nothing extra, and tapioca is exempt for everyone.
Canada: four sugar mix and dough lines (1901.20.25, .35, .60, .70) pay a 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA; no Chapter 19 line is on the September 29, 2026 import bans.
Infant formula and other dairy or sugar preparations of heading 1901 are under small tariff-rate quotas; above them the rate rises to as much as $1.035/kg + 14.9%.

Non-egg dry pasta from Italy and Türkiye also owes antidumping and countervailing deposits by producer: the 2026 final Italian rates are 2.65%–7.00% antidumping (15.45% for firms never reviewed), not the 91.74% proposed in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for biscuits and cookies?
faqs.answer: Sweet biscuits and cookies are 1905.31.00, Free under the general rate (statistical suffixes split frozen, peanut-containing and organic). Waffles and wafers are 1905.32.00, also Free; unsweetened biscuits and crackers fall in 1905.90.10 (Free). The extra duty depends on the country: none for USMCA-qualifying cookies from Canada or Mexico, 10% for the EU and the UK, 12.5% for South Korea and Türkiye, 20% for China and 37.5% for Brazil.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on Italian pasta?
faqs.answer: Dry pasta (1902.19.20) has a Free base rate, and since July 24, 2026 EU goods pay 10% in total under Section 301 (9903.05.39). Retail packs of non-egg dry pasta are also under 1996 antidumping and countervailing duty orders. The "107%" figure came from Commerce's preliminary 91.74% antidumping rate of September 2025 plus the then 15% EU tariff; the final results on March 16, 2026 set 2.65% (La Molisana), 7.00% (Garofalo) and 5.21% for 11 other firms, and countervailing rates of 3.21%–3.32% followed on July 24, 2026. Firms never reviewed pay 15.45% antidumping. Gluten-free and EU-certified organic pasta are outside the orders.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for pasta and noodles?
faqs.answer: Heading 1902. Uncooked pasta and noodles with egg are 1902.11, without egg 1902.19: Free when the product is exclusively pasta (1902.11.20, 1902.19.20), 6.4% when packed with a sauce or otherwise prepared (1902.11.40, 1902.19.40). Stuffed pasta such as ravioli and dumplings is 1902.20 (6.4%), cooked and other pasta 1902.30 (6.4%) and couscous 1902.40 (6.4%). Pasta sauce on its own is Chapter 21 (2103.90).

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for instant noodles and ramen?
faqs.answer: Instant (pre-cooked) noodles, including cup noodles and ramen with a seasoning sachet, are usually 1902.30.00 at 6.4%. Plain dry rice or wheat noodles that are only pasta are 1902.19.20 (Free). From South Korea, KORUS makes 1902.30 Free and the 12.5% Korea total applies; from Thailand or Vietnam 6.4% + 12.5% = 18.9%; from China 6.4% + 12.5% + 25% = 43.9%; from Japan 12.5% in total.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for infant formula?
searchedAs: hs tariff code for baby formula
hs code for infant formula milk powder
hs code for baby milk powder
faqs.answer: Infant formula put up for retail sale is subheading 1901.10. The U.S. line depends on milk solids, oligosaccharides and quota status: formula with over 10% milk solids containing oligosaccharides is 1901.10.11 inside a 100-tonne yearly quota (17.5%) or 1901.10.16 above it ($1.035/kg + 14.9%); formula with other dairy content is 1901.10.21/.26 on the Chapter 4 dairy quota; other formula is 1901.10.29 or 1901.10.49 (14.9%). Preparations for young children are 1901.10.52–1901.10.91. Bulk infant formula base powder is 1901.90 (for example 1901.90.62), and plain milk powder Chapter 4.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on baby formula?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on baby formula
faqs.answer: Yes. The base rate is 14.9%–17.5%, or $1.035/kg + 14.9% above the quotas, and the 2026 Section 301 duty applies by country (EU formula already above 10% pays nothing more; Australia 12.5% within its FTA dairy quota and the over-quota rate plus 12.5% above it; USMCA formula from Mexico is Free, from Canada Free inside Canada's dairy quota). The 2022 duty suspension under the Formula Act (Pub. L. 117-160, 9903.19.19–9903.19.23) expired December 31, 2022. Separately, FDA must accept the formula: 21 CFR parts 106 and 107, and the 2022 enforcement-discretion transition plan for imported formula ran to October 18, 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for breakfast cereal and granola?
faqs.answer: Cereals made by puffing or roasting, such as corn flakes and puffed rice, are 1904.10.00 (1.1%). Muesli-type mixes of unroasted flakes are 1904.20 (5.6% in airtight containers, 14.9% otherwise). Granola follows the same test — 1904.10 if all its flakes are roasted or puffed, 1904.20 if it contains unroasted flakes — and a CBP ruling settles a specific recipe. Cereal with over 6% cocoa or fully chocolate-coated moves to heading 1806. Most cereal from Canada and Mexico is Free under USMCA; from the EU it pays 10%.

faqs.question: What is HTS code 1905.90?
faqs.answer: 1905.90 is "other" bakers' wares and the largest Chapter 19 product: $7.64B of U.S. imports in 2025. 1905.90.10 (Free) covers bread, pastry, cakes, biscuits and similar baked products and puddings — split into frozen, sweet pastry, bread, organic and other. 1905.90.90 (4.5%) covers corn chips and similar savory snacks, pizza and quiche, communion wafers, rice paper and empty cachets. Headings 1905.10–1905.40 are crispbread, gingerbread, sweet biscuits, waffles and wafers, and rusks — all Free.

faqs.question: What does HS code 1901 cover?
faqs.answer: Heading 1901 is malt extract and food preparations of flour, groats, meal, starch or malt extract (under 40% cocoa) and of milk products (under 5% cocoa) not covered elsewhere. 1901.10 is retail preparations for infants and young children (infant formula), 1901.20 mixes and doughs for bakers' wares (cake, pancake and bread mixes, frozen dough), and 1901.90 malt extract, puddings, cajeta, margarine cheese and other dairy or cereal preparations. Most lines with over 10% milk solids or cane or beet sugar are quota lines.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for bread, cake and pastry — and for cake mix?
faqs.answer: Finished bread, cakes, pastry and croissants (fresh or frozen) are 1905.90.10, Free. Cake, bread and pancake mixes and unbaked doughs are 1901.20: 8.5% for plain mixes, or the quota lines when they contain over 25% butterfat or over 10% cane or beet sugar (10% in quota, 42.3¢/kg + 8.5% above). Bread flour is Chapter 11.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for crackers and wafers?
faqs.answer: Waffles and wafers, including wafer biscuits, are 1905.32.00 (Free). Unsweetened crackers are biscuits of 1905.90.10 (Free); crisp savory snacks such as corn chips are 1905.90.90.30 (4.5%). Communion wafers are 1905.90.90 (4.5%) and, when for religious purposes only, are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for pizza and tortillas?
faqs.answer: Pizza and quiche, frozen or not, are 1905.90.90.60 (4.5%), unless over 20% of the weight is meat or fish, which moves them to Chapter 16; a pizza with meat can also be a USDA FSIS product. Flour and corn tortillas are bakers' wares of 1905.90.10 (Free), and tortilla chips are crisp savory snacks of 1905.90.90.30 (4.5%). USMCA-qualifying tortillas and chips from Mexico pay nothing extra.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for couscous and tapioca pearls?
faqs.answer: Couscous is 1902.40.00 (6.4%). Tapioca pearls and flakes of cassava, arrowroot or sago are 1903.00.20 (Free), other starch substitutes 1903.00.40 (0.8¢/kg). Tapioca is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties. Tapioca starch itself is heading 1108, not Chapter 19.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for malt extract?
searchedAs: hs code for malt extract powder
hs code for liquid malt extract
faqs.answer: Malt extract is 1901.90: fluid malt extract 1901.90.10 (3.2¢/liter) and solid or condensed (powder) 1901.90.20 (9.6%). Malt itself is heading 1107. Both lines are Free for USMCA and most FTA partners, but the 2026 Section 301 duty still applies to FTA partners in the 60 economies.

faqs.question: What does HTSUS Chapter 19 cover?
faqs.answer: Chapter 19 is "Preparations of cereals, flour, starch or milk; bakers' wares": heading 1901 (malt extract, infant formula, mixes and doughs, dairy and cereal preparations), 1902 (pasta and couscous), 1903 (tapioca), 1904 (breakfast cereals, bulgur, prepared grains) and 1905 (bread, biscuits, cakes, pastry and other bakers' wares). It has 111 U.S. tariff lines, and the U.S. imported $16.12B of these goods in 2025.
